title: Teluni Pilot Deployment and Recovery Design
heading: Transactional email (PH-17 choice)
text:
Transactional email (PH-17 choice)
**Provider:** Resend's free plan through SMTP: `smtp.resend.com`, port 465 with implicit TLS (`TELUNI_MAIL_SMTP_SECURITY=tls`), user `resend`, and an API key limited to sending as the password. Reported limits are 3,000 messages a month, 100 a day and one domain, which cover the pilot's invitations and recovery.
**Sender:** a dedicated subdomain keeps the product domain's reputation separate. `TELUNI_MAIL_FROM` is `no-reply@notify.teluni.app`, with the provider's SPF and DKIM records on `notify.teluni.app`.
**DMARC:** `p=none` with aggregate reports to the owner's address for the first 30 days, then `p=quarantine` once reports show only the relay sending.
**Fallback:** Brevo's free plan through `smtp-relay.brevo.com`, reported at 300 messages a day but with its branding added. It needs only new SMTP settings, because the relay adapter is provider-neutral (ADR-0026).
**Review triggers:** the daily cap approaching 80%, bounces above 5%, or a terms change prompt a review of the provider.

title: Teluni Pilot Deployment and Recovery Design
heading: Backups and restore
text:
Backups and restore
**Tool.** restic: encrypted, deduplicated snapshots to an S3-compatible bucket, with one repository per environment. The repository password and the bucket key are host secrets. The owner keeps a copy of the repository password offline, because losing it loses every backup.
**Destination.** Backblaze B2. Its first 10 GB are reported free, and downloads are reported free up to three times the stored data, which covers restore rehearsals. restic encrypts before upload, so the provider holds only ciphertext. Cloudflare R2 is the alternative. A destination on the same host or the same disk never counts as off-host.
**What is in a snapshot:**
a `pg_dump` custom-format dump of each database (Teluni and Keycloak), taken first;
then hard links of the media volume's `objects/` tree, made on the same volume;
the release identifier and non-secret configuration names.
Secrets are excluded. They are backed up separately, as below.
**Consistency.** An object's file is written before the row that records it, and deleted only after that row is gone. Every file deletion first takes a PostgreSQL advisory lock shared, without waiting; while a backup holds it, the file stays and the hourly orphan sweep removes it later. The backup holds the lock exclusively from before its dumps until the objects are hard-linked, which takes seconds; restic then reads the links at leisure. So every object the dumps record is in the snapshot, and nobody waits for a backup. The restore check verifies it instead of assuming it.
**Schedule and retention.** A snapshot every 6 hours. `restic forget` keeps the last 8, 14 daily, and 5 weekly snapshots, then prunes weekly. No backup outlives about 35 days, which bounds how long deleted data survives in backups ([data handling policies](data-handling-policies.md)). A weekly `restic check` reads a 5% sample of the data.
**Secrets recovery.** The signing key rings, session and mail key rings, client secrets and the restic password are exported to a password manager or encrypted offline medium that the owner controls, and only when they change. Restoring a database without its key rings makes sealed mail credentials unreadable and invalidates sessions. That loss is acceptable, and it is safer than storing keys next to the data.
**Restore rehearsal.** Restore into an isolated Compose project and check:
migrations are current;
every referenced object exists with the right hash;
a test company's publication manifest resolves;
revoked sessions stay revoked (sessions older than the backup are not trusted: all sessions are terminated after a restore).
Record the achieved recovery point and time. Rehearse before the pilot and then monthly.

title: Teluni Pilot Deployment and Recovery Design
heading: Host administration and monitoring
text:
Host administration and monitoring
Debian stable with unattended security upgrades, SSH by key only and no password sign-in, a host firewall that allows only 80 and 443 (and the WireGuard port on the relay path), and full-disk encryption when the hardware allows unattended unlocking. Otherwise the database and media volumes stay on the system disk, and the threat is recorded under PH-10.
Administration over WireGuard from the owner's devices. No administrative interface is exposed publicly.
Logs: the containers' JSON logs are rotated at 14 days. They hold no personal data beyond identifiers, under the [redaction policy](../security/telemetry-redaction.md).
Minimum alerts: a failed or late backup, low disk space (below the media reserve plus 10%), a failed certificate renewal and the API health check failing for 5 minutes. All are sent by email through the same relay. An external uptime monitor is optional and not required.

title: Teluni Pilot Deployment and Recovery Design
heading: Decisions
text:
Decisions
The agent took these decisions on 2026-10-22 under the owner's delegation:
**Hostnames.** `app.teluni.app` for the panel and the API under `/api`, `auth.teluni.app` for the `teluni` realm only, and `teluni.app` redirecting to the panel.
**End-to-end TLS.** TLS ends on the owner's host. The host is reached directly when the line allows it, or through a TCP relay on a free-tier VM over WireGuard; no TLS-terminating tunnel or CDN is used (ADR-0033).
**Proxy.** Caddy 2 with automatic Let's Encrypt certificates, as the only published service. The API trusts forwarded client addresses only from it, and the relay passes them with PROXY protocol v2.
**Composition.** Four Compose services (proxy, API, Keycloak, PostgreSQL), digest-pinned images, secrets as files, one-off privileged migrations and internal networks.
**Email.** Resend's free plan over SMTP with implicit TLS from `no-reply@notify.teluni.app`, staged DMARC, and Brevo as fallback.
**Google sign-in.** One web client per environment with the Keycloak broker redirect URI and the `openid`, `email` and `profile` scopes.
**Backups.** restic snapshots every 6 hours to Backblaze B2, holding database dumps then media objects, kept for at most about 35 days, with secrets backed up separately offline (ADR-0033).
**Targets.** RPO 6 hours; RTO 4 hours with the host intact and 72 hours if it is lost; a 99% internal monthly availability objective; and the maintenance window above.
**Administration.** Key-only SSH, WireGuard administration, a minimal firewall, 14-day logs and four email alerts.

title: Teluni Pilot Deployment and Recovery Design
heading: Alternatives considered
text:
Alternatives considered
**Cloudflare Tunnel.** Free, and it removes CGNAT problems, but TLS ends at Cloudflare. The CDN terms restrict serving video and large files outside paid products, and the reported 100 MB upload cap rejects valid videos. It would also put every session cookie in a third party's path.
**A paid VPS for everything.** Removes residential risks, but contradicts the current budget. It stays the migration target in [operations](operations.md#future-host-or-storage-migration) when revenue or measured risk justifies it.
**Running the whole stack on the free-tier VM.** The free VM is subject to the provider's idle reclamation and account terms. Hosting customer data there makes those terms a single point of failure. As a relay it holds nothing and can be replaced in minutes.
**nginx with certbot, or Traefik.** Both work. Caddy needs the least configuration for automatic certificates and has no separate renewal job to monitor.
**PostgreSQL continuous archiving (WAL) for a smaller RPO.** Gives minutes of data loss, but needs a second backup mechanism and its own restore procedure. Six hours fits the pilot, and archiving can be added when a customer needs it.
**Brevo as the first email choice.** Higher daily cap, but its free plan adds branding to every message, including invitations and recovery mail.
**Backups to a second disk or another directory.** Does not survive the loss of the host, which ADR-0021 requires.

Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Status and scope
text:
Status and scope
**Approved detailed design for the server side of D-03, 2026-10-19.** The owner approved all nine [decisions for review](#decisions-for-review) as proposed under [PH-22](human-actions.md#ph-22), including ADR-0027, and asked for implementation in [PJ-08](implementation-plan.md#current-work). Approval authorizes implementation in local and CI environments with simulated players; [implementation status](#implementation-status) records what exists.
In scope: the device identity and its company/branch assignment, temporary-code enrollment, the device credential and how the API authenticates it, reported capabilities and the configured rotation (FR-03), the server's offline authorization deadline (AT-15), renaming, moving between branches, unlinking, erasure confirmation and reassignment (FR-02, P24), permissions, abuse limits, audit, data, contracts, panel workflow and verification.
Out of scope, with their owners: the Android application and its secure local storage, clock estimation and enforcement of the deadline on the device (D-07, PJ-12); signed authorization envelopes, manifests and synchronization (D-04, PJ-11); content assignment to devices and groups (PJ-10); trial, license and quota admission for enrollment (PJ-27); qualifying any hardware or orientation profile (PH-08). The design leaves explicit hooks for each and claims none of them.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Policy inputs
text:
Policy inputs
The design applies these selected policies without changing them:
Pairing codes are temporary, single-use, bound to the requesting device, rate-limited and safe under concurrent claims; the claiming person must already be authorized for the destination company and branch; a displayed code is not an enduring credential ([security requirements](security-and-i18n.md#pairing-and-device-lifecycle), FR-02).
Pairing, moving, unlinking and resetting devices is company-wide for administrators and limited to authorized source and destination branches for branch managers; operators need an additional grant ([permission matrix](identity-and-access.md#permission-model-and-default-matrix)). Administrator and branch-manager grants count only in strongly authenticated sessions (P12).
Offline authorization expires no later than seven days after its last successful online renewal (AT-15, P22); commercial deadlines may shorten it (PJ-27).
Unlink needs explicit authorized confirmation, server revocation and a distinct pending-erasure state; private content, configuration and credentials are cleared on reconnection; reassignment to another company requires verified cleanup or a controlled reset; revoked access, unreachable device and confirmed erasure stay distinct (P24).
Player identities are separate from human identities and restricted to their own assignment, media and reports. Raw codes, credentials and credential-bearing links never reach logs, errors, screenshots or support bundles. No custom cryptography or token scheme.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Mechanism overview
text:
Mechanism overview
The flow follows the shape of the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant ([RFC 8628](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628)): a device without a keyboard shows a short code, and a person who is already signed in elsewhere enters it. Teluni does not route devices through Keycloak, because devices are not human principals and Keycloak holds only human identities (ADR-0024); the API module plays both the authorization-server and resource-server role for devices.
Player                                API (devices module)                    Panel (signed-in person)
  │ generate 256-bit credential C            │                                      │
  │ POST /device-enrollments              │                                      │
  │   { credentialHash: SHA-256(C), report } │                                      │
  │ ◀── { enrollmentId, userCode, expiresAt, pollInterval }                         │
  │ show userCode on screen                  │                                      │
  │                                          │ ◀── POST /companies/{id}/devices  │
  │                                          │      { userCode, name, branch, rotation }
  │                                          │ claim: PENDING → CLAIMED, insert device
  │ POST /device-enrollments/{id}/status  │                                      │
  │   Authorization: Bearer C                │                                      │
  │ ◀── { status: "paired", deviceId }       │                                      │
  │ GET /device/self (Bearer C)  ────────▶│ configuration + authorizedUntil       │

The device generates its own credential and sends only its hash when enrollment starts. The credential itself never leaves the device until it is used, the server never returns a secret, and a lost response at any step is retried without issuing anything new. This is the central choice in [ADR-0027](../adr/0027-propose-device-generated-credentials-and-code-based-enrollment.md).

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Enrollment
text:
Enrollment
**Start.** `POST /device-enrollments` is anonymous. The body carries the credential hash (32 bytes, base64url) and the device report (see [capabilities](#capabilities-and-rotation)). The server creates a `PENDING` enrollment valid for 10 minutes and answers with the enrollment ID, the user code, the expiry and a 5-second polling interval. A hash that already belongs to a device or any enrollment is refused with `ENROLLMENT_REJECTED`, so one credential can never bind two identities.
**User code.** Eight characters from the 20-consonant alphabet `BCDFGHJKLMNPQRSTVWXZ`, shown as `XXXX-XXXX`, as RFC 8628 section 6.1 recommends: about 34.5 bits, no vowels (no accidental words) and no look-alike digits. Entry ignores case, spaces and hyphens. The server stores an HMAC-SHA-256 of the normalized code under a dedicated `RESTRICTED` key ring (key ID stored with the value, newest key first), never the code, so a database copy does not let anyone enumerate live codes offline. A unique index on the HMAC prevents two live enrollments from sharing a code; a collision on insert is retried with a new code.
**Claim.** In the panel, a person enters the code with a name, a destination branch and a rotation. In one transaction the server locks the company row (tenant data design rule 5), rebuilds the actor's access and requires `devices.manage` on the destination branch and an active company and branch, then moves the enrollment from `PENDING` to `CLAIMED` with a conditional update (`WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND expires_at > now()`), inserts the device with the enrollment's credential hash and report, and writes one `device.paired` audit event. Exactly one of two concurrent claims succeeds; the other, an expired code, a used code and an unknown code all answer the same `PAIRING_CODE_INVALID`, so the answer does not reveal which case applied. The rotation must be one the device reported as supported.
**Status.** The device polls `POST /device-enrollments/{id}/status` with `Authorization: Bearer <credential>`; the server checks the credential against the enrollment's hash. Answers are `pending` (with the polling interval), `paired` (with the device ID) or `expired`. Polling faster than the interval answers `RATE_LIMITED` with the interval to use. Pending enrollments expire lazily: reads treat an expired row as expired and a purge deletes `PENDING` rows one day after expiry, and `CLAIMED` rows 30 days after the claim.
**Commercial hook.** The claim transaction is where PJ-27 will add trial, license and quota admission. Until then only company and branch status gate enrollment.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Device credential and authentication
text:
Device credential and authentication
**Credential.** 32 bytes from the platform CSPRNG, generated and kept by the player in Android Keystore-backed storage (D-07, PJ-12). The server stores only its SHA-256 under a unique index; because the credential has 256 bits of entropy, an unkeyed hash is sufficient for lookup and gives nothing usable from a database copy. The credential is `RESTRICTED`: never in logs, telemetry, errors, audit, query strings or the panel.
**Use.** Device operations declare a new operation access kind, `device`, and expect `Authorization: Bearer <credential>` on paths under `/device/`. The devices module resolves the credential to the device on every request, with no cache, so revocation takes effect on the next request. Device routes never accept the human session cookie, and human routes never accept a device credential. The shared runtime gains only the access kind; the devices module owns the lookup.
**States.** An `ACTIVE` device's credential reaches every device operation. A `REVOKED` device's credential reaches only `GET /device/self`, which answers `{ status: "unlinked", clearRequired: true }`, and `POST /device/self/erasure`, which confirms clearing. Any other credential answers `DEVICE_UNAUTHORIZED` with no detail.
**Rotation.** `POST /device/self/credential` replaces the hash with a new device-generated one. The previous hash stays valid until the new credential is first used, so a lost response leaves the device with a working credential. Rotation is in the last delivery increment; it is not required by the first player.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Check-in and the offline authorization deadline
text:
Check-in and the offline authorization deadline
`GET /device/self` returns the device's ID, name, branch name and time zone, rotation, status and `authorizedUntil`. For an active device, `authorizedUntil` is the database clock plus seven days (AT-15), later capped by a commercial deadline under PJ-27. `PUT /device/self/report` updates the reported capabilities. Each successful device request updates `last_seen_at`, written at most once per minute per device so check-ins do not cause a write per request.
In this design `authorizedUntil` is a server statement in an authenticated HTTPS response. Making it tamper-evident on the device (a signed envelope) and enforcing it against a trusted local clock (AT-16) belong to D-04/PJ-11 and D-07/PJ-12. The panel shows "last seen" and, for unreachable devices, the latest deadline the device could hold, so operators never read server intent as device state.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Capabilities and rotation
text:
Capabilities and rotation
The device report is bounded, validated JSON: application version, protocol version, manufacturer and model (each at most 80 characters), Android version, display width and height in pixels (1 to 16384) and the supported rotations. It is stored as reported and labelled "reported by the device" in the panel; it is not a qualified hardware profile (PH-08), and nothing in this design claims support for a device because it reported a capability.
The configured orientation is a rotation of 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees clockwise: 0 and 180 are horizontal, 90 and 270 vertical (FR-03). A rotation, rather than a horizontal/vertical flag, tells the player which way the screen is physically mounted. Setting a rotation the device did not report as supported answers `ROTATION_UNSUPPORTED`; the panel offers only reported rotations.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Device lifecycle
text:
Device lifecycle
          claim                       unlink                       device confirms clearing
(none) ─────────▶ ACTIVE ───────────────────────────▶ REVOKED, erasure PENDING ───────────▶ REVOKED, erasure CONFIRMED
                  │  rename, set rotation, move           │ record controlled reset (person)
                  │  (same company only)                  └──────────────────────────────▶ REVOKED, erasure RESET_RECORDED

**Rename and rotation.** Need `devices.manage` on the device's branch and the expected version.
**Move.** Changes the branch within the same company. Needs `devices.manage` on both the source and the destination branch, an active destination branch and the expected version. Moving to another company is not an operation: it is an unlink followed by a new enrollment.
**Unlink.** Needs `devices.manage` on the device's branch, the expected version and an explicit confirmation in the panel that names the device. It sets `REVOKED` with erasure `PENDING` in one transaction; from then on the credential reaches only the two operations above. It cannot be undone; the device is paired again with a new enrollment.
**Erasure confirmation.** When an unlinked device reconnects, it learns `clearRequired`, deletes private content, configuration and its credential locally (PJ-12), and only then calls `POST /device/self/erasure` with the credential it is about to discard. The server records `CONFIRMED`, deletes the credential hash and writes `device.erasure_confirmed`. If the response is lost, the device has already cleared and the record stays `PENDING`, shown honestly as unconfirmed, which is the safe direction.
**Controlled reset.** A device that will never reconnect (factory reset, broken, lost) stays `PENDING`. A person with `devices.manage` can record that the device was reset locally; the record says `RESET_RECORDED` with the actor, not `CONFIRMED`, and audit keeps the difference.
**Reassignment.** The server cannot recognize a physical device across identities, so verified cleanup is enforced where it can be: the player starts a new enrollment only from a state with no credential and no private content, and when it still holds a credential it first completes the erasure confirmation above. A new enrollment always creates a new device identity; the old record keeps its own history. The panel lists unlinked devices with their erasure state until the purge below.
Archived branches keep their devices; archiving a branch that still has active devices answers `BRANCH_IN_USE`, through a guard the devices module registers on the organizations access port, so a device is never left in a branch nobody can manage.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Permissions
text:
Permissions
Two capabilities are added to the organizations domain, which owns role presets:

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Abuse limits
text:
Abuse limits
Proposed initial values:
Enrollment start: the existing per-route rate limit plus at most 20 starts per client address per hour, and at most 10,000 pending enrollments platform-wide, after which starts answer `RATE_LIMITED`. A full pending table makes a guessed code at most 10,000 in 2.56 × 10¹⁰ likely to match.
Claim: at most 10 failed claims per person per 15 minutes and 30 per company per 15 minutes, counted in PostgreSQL from failed-claim rows that record only the actor, company and time. Exceeding a limit answers `RATE_LIMITED` without saying which applied. With these limits an attacker with one account needs on the order of years of attempts per expected match against a full pending table. Many accounts or companies created for guessing remain a residual risk that the signup abuse controls (PH-13) must bound; a successful guess pairs a stranger's screen to the attacker's company, which its owner notices because pairing fails on their side, and no tenant data is exposed.
Status polling: once per polling interval per enrollment.
The per-address limit uses the address Fastify reports for the connection, as the identity routes do; behind a reverse proxy it counts the proxy until trusted forwarding is configured for the production deployment. The general request limit of device routes counts each presented credential instead, under a ceiling of 6,000 requests per address per minute, so screens sharing an address do not exhaust it for each other.
These limits stand on their own; commercial device quotas are PJ-27.

Data

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Contracts
text:
Contracts
Human operations (session access, CSRF as elsewhere): `GET /companies/{companyId}/devices` (paginated, cursor-bound, filter by branch and status), `GET .../devices/{deviceId}`, `POST .../devices` (claim), `PATCH .../devices/{deviceId}` (name, rotation, expected version), `POST .../devices/{deviceId}/move`, `POST .../devices/{deviceId}/unlink`, `POST .../devices/{deviceId}/reset-record`. Device operations: the enrollment start and status, `GET /device/self`, `PUT /device/self/report`, `POST /device/self/erasure` and, later, `POST /device/self/credential`. All are TypeBox contracts in the OpenAPI document; the web uses the generated SDK. New expected errors: `PAIRING_CODE_INVALID`, `ENROLLMENT_REJECTED`, `ROTATION_UNSUPPORTED`, `DEVICE_UNAUTHORIZED`, `DEVICE_UNLINKED` (a human change of an unlinked device), `DEVICE_ERASURE_NOT_PENDING` (a reset record without pending erasure), `BRANCH_IN_USE` (organizations), plus the existing `RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND`, `RESOURCE_VERSION_CONFLICT`, `RATE_LIMITED` and strong-authentication errors.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Panel
text:
Panel
A **Screens** view per company (pt-BR "Telas") lists devices with name, branch, status, rotation, last seen and erasure state, filtered to what the person may view. **Pair a screen** asks for the code shown on the TV, a name, a branch the person may manage and a rotation, and shows the reported model and resolution after a successful claim. The device page renames, changes rotation, moves (destinations limited to manageable branches), unlinks with a confirmation naming the device, and records a reset for a pending erasure. Conflicts and unknown outcomes reload and explain, as other company pages do. Copy is in `pt-BR` and `en-US`.

Contract tests for every expected error and the device access kind; no route accepts the wrong credential type.
Browser component tests for the pairing form, the list and the unlink confirmation, and one end-to-end journey that simulates the player over HTTP: start enrollment, pair in the panel, check in, unlink and confirm erasure.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Decisions for review
text:
Decisions for review
The owner approved each item as proposed on 2026-10-19 under [PH-22](human-actions.md#ph-22):
**Enrollment mechanism (ADR-0027).** RFC 8628-style flow owned by the API: the device shows a short code and polls; a signed-in person claims the code in the panel. Devices do not use Keycloak.
**Device-generated credential.** The player generates a 256-bit credential and sends only its SHA-256 at enrollment; the server stores only the hash, never issues a secret and accepts it as a bearer token on device routes only, checked on every request.
**User code.** Eight characters from 20 consonants (`XXXX-XXXX`), valid 10 minutes, single use, stored as a keyed HMAC under a new `RESTRICTED` key ring; every failure answers the same error.
**Abuse limits.** 20 enrollment starts per address per hour, 10,000 pending platform-wide, 10 failed claims per person and 30 per company per 15 minutes, polling once per interval.
**Offline deadline.** Check-in reports `authorizedUntil` as server time plus seven days (AT-15); signing and device-side enforcement are left to PJ-11/PJ-12, and commercial capping to PJ-27.
**Rotation and capabilities.** Rotation of 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees limited to what the device reports; reports are stored as device statements, not qualified support.
**Unlink and reassignment.** Unlink is immediate, irreversible revocation with erasure `PENDING`; the revoked credential can only learn it must clear and confirm clearing; a person may record a controlled reset, shown distinctly from confirmation; another company always pairs a new identity, and the player enrolls only from a cleared state.
**Permissions.** `devices.view` for all roles in their scope; `devices.manage` for administrators company-wide and branch managers on their branches (both branches for a move); operators need a future additional grant.
**Retention (provisional until PH-13).** Unclaimed enrollments deleted one day after expiry, claimed enrollments 30 days after the claim, failed-claim counters after one day; device records and audit are kept with the company; network addresses are never stored.
Approval authorizes implementation of PJ-08 in local and CI environments with simulated players. It does not select hardware (PH-08), implement the Android player (PJ-12) or qualify any physical behavior.

title: Teluni Device Enrollment and Lifecycle Design
heading: Alternatives considered
text:
Alternatives considered
**Server-issued credential returned once on pairing.** Simpler for the device, but the only copy travels in a response that can be lost, which forces either a re-issue path (more secret-bearing responses) or a stuck device. Rejected in favor of the device-generated credential.
**Device key pair with signed requests (for example DPoP, RFC 9449, or mutual TLS).** Stronger against a copied credential because the private key can stay in Android Keystore hardware, but it adds JWT/proof verification or certificate infrastructure on a single-host pilot with no measured threat requiring it. ADR-0027 keeps the bearer credential behind the `device` access kind so a proof-of-possession scheme can replace it later without changing the enrollment flow.
**Keycloak device grant and service accounts.** Reuses an established implementation, but makes every screen a Keycloak client or user, couples player availability to Keycloak and mixes device and human identities, which the policies keep separate.
**Numeric six-digit codes.** Easier to type on a remote but only about 20 bits; with the same limits an attacker would match a pending code orders of magnitude sooner.
**QR code with a link.** Convenient on phones but puts a credential-bearing link on screen and in browser history; it can be added later as another way to enter the same short code.

[x] **Require pull requests and the CI gate on this repository's default branch, and keep merge commits available.**
**Status:** completed. **Owner:** repository administrator.
**Dependency / trigger:** PH-01; [PJ-01](implementation-plan.md#current-work).
**Request and reason:** Protect `main`: require pull requests and the `Orion required gate` status check, block force pushes and deletion, and review bypass actors. Keep merge commits allowed and do not require linear history on `main`, because Orion upgrade pull requests must be merged with a merge commit to preserve upstream ancestry ([upgrade workflow](../project-derivation.md#upgrade-to-a-newer-orion-revision)). Branch protection is repository administration that local automation cannot perform.
**Configuration:** none beyond the repository ruleset and merge settings.
**Verification:** Read the effective rules for `main` and confirm the required check name matches [CI](../../.github/workflows/ci.yml) and that no linear-history requirement applies; confirm merge commits are allowed; a successful required-gate run appears on a pull request.
**Evidence / blocker:** 2026-10-17: verified through the GitHub API that active [ruleset 25323352, Protect main](https://github.com/GabriellMDias/teluni/rules/25323352) targets the default branch `main`, requires pull requests and the `Orion required gate` check from GitHub Actions (integration 15368), blocks deletion and non-fast-forward updates, has no bypass actors, and does not require linear history. Merge commits are allowed in both the repository settings and the ruleset. [CI run 39077703462](https://github.com/GabriellMDias/teluni/actions/runs/39077703462) succeeded for push commit `c9193734d5f5de22883af433d48006805fb86604`, including `Validate` and `Orion required gate`. [PR #2](https://github.com/GabriellMDias/teluni/pull/2) then exercised the pull-request workflow: [run 39078757654](https://github.com/GabriellMDias/teluni/actions/runs/39078757654) passed `Validate` and `Orion required gate` for head commit `98a87a896fce6126566ba1521c8954b1fdb5866a`. Configuration and successful PR-gate verification are complete. No repository settings were changed during verification.

title: Teluni Human Actions
heading: PH-10

PH-10
[ ] **Confirm residential-host feasibility, exposure and recovery commitments before a real pilot.**
**Status:** pending. **Owner:** project owner / server and network administrator.
**Dependency / trigger:** PJ-07/PJ-13 and before PJ-14 real-customer operation.
**Request and reason:** Supply the host/network inventory: whether the line has a public IPv4 address or is behind CGNAT, whether inbound 443 reaches the router, IPv6, upload bandwidth, data caps, power and reboot behavior, CPU/RAM/disk. Create the accounts the [deployment design](deployment-design.md) needs: the relay VM only if the line requires it, and the off-host backup bucket. Keep the restic password offline. Then run the restore rehearsal on the real host. The exposure path, proxy, backup method, RPO/RTO, availability objective and maintenance window are decided there. Support coverage stays with PH-18. Review the [deployment readiness gates](operations.md#residential-exposure-and-readiness-gate).
**Configuration:** only currently implemented names from the [configuration reference](../generated/configuration/api.md); new deployment keys are pending design. Put secrets only in an approved protected destination.
**Verification:** Network/ingress/security inspection and isolated timed PostgreSQL-plus-media restore, followed by reboot/offline and endpoint-migration rehearsal with supported players.
**Evidence / blocker:** No cloud budget; personal residential server intended. 2026-10-22: under the owner's delegation the agent decided the [deployment design](deployment-design.md) and ADR-0033: end-to-end TLS on the host through Caddy, direct or through a WireGuard TCP relay; restic snapshots every 6 hours to Backblaze B2, kept about 35 days; RPO 6 hours, RTO 4 hours with the host intact and 72 hours if it is lost; a 99% internal objective; and a weekday 02:00–06:00 maintenance window. Host facts, accounts and the real rehearsal remain unverified. No deployment authorized by this entry.

title: Teluni Human Actions
heading: PH-15
text:
PH-15
[ ] **Prepare controlled self-hosted identity resources and protected provisioning inputs.**
**Status:** pending. **Owner:** project owner / identity and server administrator.
**Dependency / trigger:** PH-10, completed PH-11 architectural selection and the reviewed PJ-24 implementation design; before provider integration or real identity use.
**Request and reason:** Confirm host capacity, a controlled HTTPS issuer address, restricted provider administration, persistent provider storage and protected signing/recovery material. Identify responsible administrators and safe recovery ownership without publishing personal account details. Prepare inputs only after the reviewed provider/version design; this action does not authorize deployment.
**Configuration:** the [configuration reference](../generated/configuration/api.md) defines the token settings `ORION_TOKEN_ISSUER`, `ORION_TOKEN_AUDIENCE` and `ORION_TOKEN_JWKS_URL` and the human identity settings `TELUNI_PUBLIC_ORIGIN`, `TELUNI_OIDC_CLIENT_ID`, `TELUNI_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET`, `TELUNI_IDENTITY_PROVISIONER_CLIENT_ID`, `TELUNI_IDENTITY_PROVISIONER_CLIENT_SECRET` and `TELUNI_SESSION_KEYS` (the three secrets are `RESTRICTED`). The realm and clients they refer to are created by `apps/api/scripts/identity-realm.ts`, and the realm's `teluni` login theme must be installed in the deployed Keycloak (`apps/api/keycloak/themes/teluni` plus the brand mark and typeface listed by `teluniThemeFiles()`). Supply secret material only in an approved protected destination, never in this checklist or chat.
**Verification:** Record non-secret environment/issuer ownership and controlled access; during authorized implementation verify pinned provider, human-only claim provisioning, key rotation, restricted management and isolated revocation-safe restore under PH-10/PJ-13.
**Evidence / blocker:** 2026-10-18: self-hosting/Keycloak accepted by the owner; Keycloak 26.8.1 source was reviewed for compatibility, but host capacity, actual deployment version/image, issuer control, secret destination and deployment remain unverified. Foundation validation is not provisioning evidence. 2026-10-22: under the owner's delegation the [deployment design](deployment-design.md#identity-in-a-real-environment) decided the issuer `https://auth.teluni.app/realms/teluni`, the production Keycloak service (`start`, PostgreSQL storage, the pinned digest, admin console reachable only over the administration tunnel) and secrets as root-only files. Running it with the protected inputs remains.

title: Teluni Human Actions
heading: PH-17
text:
PH-17
[ ] **Establish a verified transactional-email path for identity invitations and recovery.**
**Status:** pending. **Owner:** project owner / domain and mail administrator.
**Dependency / trigger:** PH-07 domain control, PH-10 hosting, PH-11 flow review and PH-13 notices; before public signup or real invitations/recovery in PJ-24.

Confirm the provider's current limits and terms. Review required DNS authentication, deliverability, abuse response and sender continuity; do not assume residential SMTP or an unspecified free service is adequate. If no suitable path exists, record the budget/readiness blocker rather than bypassing verification/recovery.
**Configuration:** the [configuration reference](../generated/configuration/api.md) defines `TELUNI_MAIL_SMTP_HOST`, `TELUNI_MAIL_SMTP_PORT`, `TELUNI_MAIL_SMTP_SECURITY` (TLS required in production), `TELUNI_MAIL_SMTP_USERNAME`, `TELUNI_MAIL_SMTP_PASSWORD` (`RESTRICTED`), `TELUNI_MAIL_FROM` and the `RESTRICTED` key ring `TELUNI_MAIL_KEYS`; Keycloak's realm SMTP settings for its own mail are written by the realm provisioning script. Credentials go only in the approved protected store. Do not publish credentials, reset or invitation links, or private recipient records.
**Verification:** Authorized implementation tests delivery/failure/retry and invitation/reset expiry/single-use behavior with synthetic addresses under actual approved sender configuration. DNS/service/account facts need owner evidence; documentation is not delivery proof.
**Evidence / blocker:** 2026-10-18: P03=A confirms no recurring identity/email procurement now. No existing sender, delivery service, DNS configuration or successful delivery is established. The approved [invitation and email delivery design](invitation-delivery-design.md) ([PH-21](#ph-21)) requires only authenticated SMTP submission with TLS from the chosen service, shared by the application and Keycloak. 2026-10-22: under the owner's delegation the agent chose the provider and sender in the [deployment design](deployment-design.md#transactional-email-ph-17-choice): Resend over SMTP with implicit TLS from `no-reply@notify.teluni.app`, DMARC `p=none` for 30 days then `p=quarantine`, and Brevo as fallback. The account, DNS verification, key and a real delivery test remain.

text:
PH-21
[x] **Review and approve the proposed D-13 invitation and durable email delivery design and ADR-0026.**
**Status:** completed. **Owner:** project owner, with engineering/security review.
**Dependency / trigger:** [PJ-30](implementation-plan.md#current-work); blocks the invitation work remaining in PJ-03, which every real onboarding of a second person into a company needs. Real sending to real people additionally remains gated by [PH-17](#ph-17) and [PH-13](#ph-13).
**Request and reason:** Read the [invitation and email delivery design](invitation-delivery-design.md) and the proposed [ADR-0026](../adr/0026-propose-a-postgresql-outbox-and-smtp-relay-for-transactional-email.md), then approve, reject or adjust each of the design's [ten decisions for review](invitation-delivery-design.md#decisions-for-review): (1) a PostgreSQL outbox written in the producer's transaction, an in-process dispatcher and a provider-neutral SMTP relay through `nodemailer`, with no broker, worker service, provider API or webhooks; (2) at-least-once delivery with up to eight attempts over about 22 hours and failures shown to the inviter; (3) a 256-bit credential stored as a hash, an encrypted delivery copy erased at the message's final state, and the link credential in the URL fragment; (4) acceptance only by a session whose verified email equals the recipient, with no email lookup at invitation time and, until signup exists, only existing verified accounts; (5) active members gain the invited grant, suspended members are refused, removed people return as a new membership (membership uniqueness then excludes removed rows); (6) revalidation at acceptance with no silent narrowing, so a responsibility transfer invalidates the former responsible administrator's pending administrator invitations; (7) who may invite whom, grant expiry, one pending invitation per address and resend replacing it; (8) limits of 50 invitations per company per day, 100 pending per company and 3 emails per address per day, with fixed `pt-BR`/`en-US` templates and no free text; (9) provisional retention of 30 days for message rows and 90 days for invitation addresses after final state, never storing addresses in audit; (10) Keycloak keeps sending its own mail synchronously through the same relay. These are security, privacy and delivery choices with long-lived consequences that the repository requires the owner, not an agent, to approve.
**Configuration:** none. The design names configuration concepts only (relay host/port/TLS mode/username, a `RESTRICTED` relay password, sender address/name and a `RESTRICTED` outbound-mail key ring); settings are added to the canonical configuration schema when implemented. No real relay credentials are needed for local or CI work, which uses Mailpit.
**Verification:** Record the owner's dated explicit decision per item (chat or pull-request review). On approval, mark the design approved and ADR-0026 accepted, complete PJ-30 and resume the PJ-03 invitation increments. A rejected or changed item updates the design and, where it changes the delivery mechanism, ADR-0026 or a new ADR.
**Evidence / blocker:** 2026-10-18: the owner asked for this design for approval; the design and ADR-0026 were drafted and linked from the plan, the product architecture and the decision index. The same day the owner explicitly approved all ten decisions as proposed, including ADR-0026, in chat, and asked to proceed to implementing invitations. This approves the design and the delivery mechanism for local and CI work with synthetic addresses and Mailpit. It does not choose the real provider or sender (PH-17), set legal retention (PH-13) or authorize sending to real people.

heading: PH-27
text:
PH-27
[ ] **Create and keep the player's release signing key.**
**Status:** pending. **Owner:** project owner.
**Dependency / trigger:** [PJ-12](implementation-plan.md#current-work) increment 4 and any APK installed on a pilot screen. It does not block development or CI, which build debug or unsigned release APKs.
**Request and reason:** Android accepts an update only when it is signed with the same key as the installed app, so the key that signs the first pilot APK must sign every later release. It must stay outside the repository and agent sessions. Create an RSA 4096 or EC P-256 key in a PKCS12 keystore (for example with `keytool -genkeypair -keystore teluni-player-release.p12 -storetype PKCS12 -alias teluni-player -keyalg RSA -keysize 4096 -validity 10000`). Keep it with two offline backups, and record only the certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint in the player's installation guide. Losing the key means every screen must be reset and reinstalled.
**Configuration:** the release build will read the keystore path, alias and passwords from Gradle properties or environment variables that the player README names when release signing is implemented; never commit their values.
**Verification:** The fingerprint is recorded, an APK signed by the release process verifies with `apksigner verify --print-certs` against it, and an update signed with the same key installs over the previous release on a test device.
**Evidence / blocker:** 2026-10-20: requested by the [player design](player-design.md#updates-and-compatibility); no key exists yet.
